description: Team Terrarium brings a senior physicist who sees thermal inertia in every rock, and two software engineers, a senior and a third-year, who turn satellite pixels into living maps. We hunt for the Moon and Mars hidden in Mongolia’s lava fields, permafrost and deserts. TERRA-TWIN is the result: a tool ranking Mongolian landscapes as training grounds for Artemis and Mars.
summary:
We built TERRA-TWIN, an interactive decision-support platform powered by our Analog Fidelity Index (AFIX)—a quantitative framework that evaluates seven understudied Mongolian landscapes against NASA Moon and Mars mission data. Rather than relying on visual guesswork, we fuse 14 open Earth, lunar, and Martian datasets to score each site across four critical physical dimensions: thermal behavior, surface chemistry, soil mechanics, and landform geometry.

Our platform directly solves the challenge by turning raw planetary science into an actionable mission planner. Because no single Earth site mimics every off-world condition, our Mission Ranker lets researchers dynamically re-weight physical criteria for specific goals—such as rover mobility, geochemistry, or cold-soak hardware testing—while adjusting for real-world seasonal access and data confidence.

Why it matters: While analog research repeatedly defaults to places like the Atacama or Iceland, Mongolia packs extreme continental cold, young basaltic lava tubes, permafrost, dunes, and a drilled impact crater into one accessible transect. TERRA-TWIN proves where these sites excel (such as Tabun-Khara-Obo crater and Khorgo for robotic and geological trials) and explicitly maps where Earth falls short, giving space agencies a practical blueprint to test hardware and reduce mission risks before launch.
details:
Project Overview & How It Works 

We built TERRA-TWIN, an interactive mission-planning platform powered by the Analog Fidelity Index (AFIX)—a quantitative framework that evaluates seven understudied Mongolian landscapes against lunar and Martian reference regions. Rather than relying on surface-level visual comparisons, our two-stage geospatial pipeline fuses 14 open datasets from NASA, ESA, and ground surveys to score each site across four physical dimensions: thermal behavior (S_therm), surface chemistry (S_geol), soil mechanics (S_rheo), and landform geometry (S_morph). We then apply real-world modifiers for evidence confidence (E) and seasonal field accessibility (A) to generate an adjusted practicality score (AFIX), turning raw geological metrics into an objective, ranked expedition guide.

Benefits & Intended Impact While global space research repeatedly defaults to the Atacama, Iceland, or Antarctica, Mongolia packs extreme continental cold, young basaltic lava tubes, active dunes, alkaline lakes, and a drilled impact crater into one accessible country. TERRA-TWIN provides mission planners with a rigorous decision-making tool that pinpoints exactly what each site can—and cannot—teach us. Our analysis proves that while Mongolia cannot replicate extreme lunar or Martian night temperatures, sites like Tabun-Khara-Obo crater and the Khorgo volcanic complex offer world-class testing grounds for rover mobility, subsurface radar calibration, and cold-weather hardware operations. By mapping both high-value research targets and critical field data gaps, our project establishes a standardized blueprint to de-risk future Moon and Mars missions before launch.

Tools, Data & Technical Architecture To develop TERRA-TWIN, we integrated Mongolian geological surveys, borehole logs, and NOAA climate records with planetary mission datasets from NASA’s LRO Diviner, Apollo, Curiosity, InSight, MRO, and Perseverance. For macro-screening and orbital visualization, we leveraged Earth-observation archives including MODIS, ASTER, ERA5, Sentinel-2, and Copernicus DEM, alongside live weather telemetry via the Meteomatics API.

Creativity & Strategic Considerations What makes TERRA-TWIN uniquely creative is its rejection of a one-size-fits-all "best analog" label. Through our interactive Mission Ranker, researchers can dynamically shift weights across six mission profiles—from rover traction trials at Khongoryn Els to ground-ice drilling in the Darkhad Depression—and watch site rankings update instantaneously. Furthermore, our team grounded the platform in operational realism: we explicitly account for Earth's physical limits (such as gravity, vacuum, and radiation) alongside practical field constraints like national park permits, winter ice blockages, and the distinction between verified borehole truth and textbook proxies, ensuring engineers know precisely how to compensate when translating Earth trials to off-world environments.
